countries.name: China
countries.slate_detail: Medium & heavy sour import blend — Saudi Arab Light/Heavy, Russian ESPO & Urals, Iranian Heavy, Iraqi Basrah, Brazilian pre-salt
countries.note: World's largest refiner since 2023. Record 11.6 mb/d of crude imports in 2025, of which at least 2.6 mb/d sanctioned. New coastal complexes (Zhoushan, Yulong, Hengli) are deep-conversion and petrochemical-integrated; Shandong teapots are simpler but numerous.

countries.name: United States
countries.slate_detail: Barbell: domestic light sweet shale (WTI ~40° API) plus imported heavy sour (WCS 20.5°, Maya 21.5°)
countries.note: Capacity fell from 18.45 to 18.2 mb/d over 2025 as LyondellBasell Houston and Phillips 66 Los Angeles closed. 130 operable refineries. Gulf Coast averages >13 Nelson — the deepest conversion fleet in the world.

countries.name: Russia
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Urals (31° API, ~1.6% S), Siberian Light, ESPO
countries.note: Nameplate only. Essentially every major refinery in European Russia was struck by drones between 2025 and mid-2026; reported losses have reached ~25% of capacity, triggering fuel export bans. Omsk and Angarsk remain unhit.

countries.name: India
countries.slate_detail: Heavy sour by design — Basrah Heavy, Urals, Venezuelan Merey, West African and US grades opportunistically
countries.note: Jamnagar (Reliance) runs at a Nelson index near 21, the highest in the world. Nayara's Vadinar plant, 49% Rosneft-owned, was sanctioned by the EU in 2025. India is the marginal buyer of discounted heavy sour.

countries.name: South Korea
countries.slate_detail: Middle East medium and heavy sour — Saudi, Kuwaiti, UAE — plus condensate splitters
countries.note: Four very large, very complex complexes (Ulsan, Yeosu, Onsan, Daesan). Export-oriented; among the highest average complexity of any national fleet.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
countries.slate_detail: Own Arab Light (33°/1.8% S), Arab Medium and Arab Heavy (27°/2.9% S)
countries.note: Aramco has added SATORP, Jazan and equity stakes abroad (Motiva Port Arthur, S-Oil, Fujian). Strategy is to place its own sour barrels into refineries it controls.

countries.name: Japan
countries.slate_detail: Middle East medium sour, largely Saudi and UAE term barrels
countries.note: Structurally shrinking with domestic demand; capacity has fallen by roughly a third since 2000. Moderate complexity, strong desulphurisation but limited coking.

countries.name: Iran
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Iranian Heavy (30°/~2% S) and Light, plus Persian Gulf Star condensate
countries.note: Persian Gulf Star is one of the world's largest condensate refineries. Sanctions constrain catalyst and equipment supply more than crude availability.

countries.name: Brazil
countries.slate_detail: Domestic pre-salt: Tupi/Lula and Búzios, ~29° API but unusually low sulphur (~0.3%)
countries.note: Petrobras crude is medium-density yet sweet — an awkward fit for a fleet built for it, and increasingly exported to China while Brazil imports products.

countries.name: Germany
countries.slate_detail: Post-2022 mix of WTI, Norwegian, Kazakh CPC and West African, replacing Urals
countries.note: Schwedt (PCK), under German trusteeship of Rosneft's stake, was engineered for Urals via Druzhba and has struggled since. BP shut a third of Gelsenkirchen; Shell closed Wesseling in 2025.

countries.name: Canada
countries.slate_detail: Western Canadian Select (20.5°/3.5% S) and synthetic crude in the west; imported light sweet in the east
countries.note: Average Nelson just above 8 — less heavy-capable than the US Midwest despite producing the heavy barrel. Irving Saint John, the largest plant, runs imported grades.

countries.name: Italy
countries.slate_detail: Mediterranean sour grades, Iraqi, Kazakh and Libyan barrels
countries.note: ISAB Priolo in Sicily — formerly Lukoil-owned, forcibly sold in 2023 — is one of Europe's few genuinely deep-conversion plants.

countries.name: Spain
countries.slate_detail: Heavy sour including Mexican Maya, plus US WTI and West African grades
countries.note: Repsol and Moeve (ex-Cepsa) run one of Europe's most complex fleets: Cartagena and Bilbao have real coking capacity, unusual for the continent.

countries.name: Mexico
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Maya (21.5°/3.6% S), Isthmus and Olmeca
countries.note: Chronic underutilisation. The new 340 kb/d Olmeca refinery at Dos Bocas was intended to consume Maya domestically; its slow ramp has kept those barrels flowing to the US Gulf.

countries.name: Kuwait
countries.slate_detail: Kuwait Export Blend (31°/2.5% S) and heavier domestic streams
countries.note: Al-Zour (615 kb/d) was purpose-built to convert high-sulphur residue into IMO-compliant low-sulphur fuel oil — one of the most consequential new plants of the decade.

countries.name: Venezuela
countries.slate_detail: Extra-heavy Merey 16 and Boscan (~10° API, 5.5% S) blended with imported diluent
countries.note: Nameplate is fiction: the Paraguaná complex and Puerto La Cruz have run at a small fraction of capacity for years. The crude itself needs upgraders as much as refineries.

countries.name: Singapore
countries.slate_detail: Fully imported — Middle East sour, regional sweet, condensate
countries.note: Pure refining and petrochemical hub with no domestic crude. Shell's Bukom sale to Chandra Asri/Glencore in 2024 marked the end of an era for Western majors in the region.

countries.name: United Arab Emirates
countries.slate_detail: Murban (40°/0.75% S) — light but slightly sour — and Upper Zakum medium sour
countries.note: Ruwais (817 kb/d) is among the largest single sites in the world. Murban's promotion to a futures benchmark in 2021 was a deliberate move to price the UAE's own barrel.

countries.name: Indonesia
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Minas/Duri plus Middle East and West African imports
countries.note: Duri is a rarity: heavy (21° API) but almost sulphur-free. Pertamina's fleet is old and under a long-running upgrade programme.

countries.name: Thailand
countries.slate_detail: Middle East sour with regional sweet blending
countries.note: Medium complexity; refiners are integrated with domestic petrochemicals.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.slate_detail: North Sea, West African and Middle East grades via Rotterdam
countries.note: Shell Pernis (~400 kb/d) is the largest refinery in Europe. Rotterdam is the continent's product blending and storage hub as much as a refining centre.

countries.name: Iraq
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Basrah Medium (29°/2.9% S) and Basrah Heavy (24°/4% S)
countries.note: Low average complexity and heavy fuel oil surplus. Basrah Heavy is one of the sourest widely traded grades and prices accordingly.

countries.name: Taiwan
countries.slate_detail: Middle East sour term barrels
countries.note: Formosa's Mailiao complex (~540 kb/d) is fully petrochemical-integrated; CPC runs the rest.

countries.name: Malaysia
countries.slate_detail: Regional sweet (Tapis, Miri) plus Middle East sour at Pengerang
countries.note: Pengerang RAPID (300 kb/d) is modern and complex; Aramco exited its stake in 2025 after years of dispute.

countries.name: France
countries.slate_detail: West African, North Sea and Kazakh grades
countries.note: TotalEnergies has converted Grandpuits and La Mède away from crude; Gonfreville and Donges carry the remaining fleet.

countries.name: Nigeria
countries.slate_detail: Light sweet — Bonny Light (35°/0.15% S), Qua Iboe, plus imported WTI Midland and Libyan Sharara
countries.note: Dangote (650 kb/d) accounts for nearly all functioning capacity; the NNPC plants at Port Harcourt, Warri and Kaduna have been largely non-operational for years. Feedstock security, not conversion depth, is the constraint.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.slate_detail: North Sea light sweet plus imported grades
countries.note: Down sharply: Grangemouth (150 kb/d) stopped processing crude in 2025 and Prax Lindsey entered administration. Five refineries remain, led by Fawley and Humber — the latter one of the few dedicated to petroleum coke.

countries.name: Egypt
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Western Desert and Gulf of Suez crude plus imports
countries.note: Largest African fleet by plant count; MIDOR at Alexandria is the most modern.

countries.name: Turkey
countries.slate_detail: Was a large Urals buyer; now a mix of Russian, Iraqi and Kazakh grades
countries.note: Tüpraş's İzmit and İzmir plants plus SOCAR's STAR at Aliağa. Turkey became a major re-exporter of products refined from discounted Russian crude after 2022.

countries.name: Algeria
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Saharan Blend (45°/0.09% S) — among the lightest, sweetest crudes traded
countries.note: Sonatrach's fleet is simple by design; it does not need conversion depth for this feed.

countries.name: Belgium
countries.slate_detail: North Sea and West African grades via Antwerp
countries.note: TotalEnergies Antwerp is one of the more complex plants in northern Europe, tightly integrated with the port's petrochemical cluster.

countries.name: Argentina
countries.slate_detail: Increasingly Vaca Muerta light sweet (Medanito, ~35°/0.5% S) displacing Escalante heavy
countries.note: Domestic shale growth is reversing decades of crude imports; refiners are re-tuning toward lighter feed.

countries.name: Poland
countries.slate_detail: Saudi Arab Light and Norwegian grades, replacing Urals from 2023
countries.note: Orlen's Płock (~327 kb/d) and Gdańsk. One of the more decisive European pivots away from Russian feedstock, achieved largely through Aramco term contracts.

countries.name: Greece
countries.slate_detail: Mediterranean and Middle East sour, historically Iranian and Russian
countries.note: Motor Oil Corinth and HelleniQ Elefsina are relatively complex for their size and export heavily.

countries.name: Colombia
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Castilla Blend (18.8°/2% S) and Vasconia
countries.note: Cartagena's post-2015 upgrade gave Ecopetrol genuine heavy-crude capability.

countries.name: Belarus
countries.slate_detail: Russian Urals via Druzhba
countries.note: Mozyr and Naftan were built as export refineries for the Soviet system and remain wholly dependent on Russian crude.

countries.name: Sweden
countries.slate_detail: North Sea and Russian-free imports since 2022
countries.note: Preem's Lysekil is the largest and, unusually for Europe, has real conversion depth.

countries.name: Pakistan
countries.slate_detail: Middle East sour, mostly Saudi and UAE term supply
countries.note: Small, simple plants with persistent furnace-oil surplus.

countries.name: Kazakhstan
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Tengiz and Karachaganak light sour; CPC Blend (45°/0.55% S) is exported
countries.note: Atyrau, Pavlodar and Shymkent were modernised in the late 2010s. Pavlodar is configured for West Siberian crude.

countries.name: Bahrain
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Bahrain field plus Saudi Arab Light via pipeline
countries.note: The Sitra modernisation lifted capacity and complexity substantially, completing a wave of ~1.4 mb/d of new GCC capacity.

countries.name: Libya
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Es Sider (37°/0.45% S) and Sharara (43°/0.07% S)
countries.note: Zawia and Ras Lanuf are damaged and partly idle; Libya exports crude and imports products. Sharara has become a swing feedstock for Dangote.

countries.name: Vietnam
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Bach Ho sweet at Dung Quat; Kuwaiti sour at Nghi Son
countries.note: Nghi Son was built around a Kuwaiti crude supply agreement — a supply-security design, not a market one.

countries.name: Qatar
countries.slate_detail: Largely condensate from the North Field, plus some crude
countries.note: Ras Laffan's condensate splitters dominate; the coming Laffan expansion is naphtha- and jet-oriented.

countries.name: Curaçao
countries.slate_detail: Venezuelan Merey, historically
countries.note: The Isla refinery was leased by PDVSA for decades and has been effectively idle since 2019. Nameplate only.

countries.name: Israel
countries.slate_detail: Azeri BTC and Kazakh grades via the Mediterranean
countries.note: Haifa and Ashdod; Haifa faces long-running pressure to close on environmental grounds.

countries.name: Oman
countries.slate_detail: Oman Blend (33°/1.2% S) plus Kuwaiti crude at Duqm
countries.note: OQ8's Duqm refinery (230 kb/d), a joint venture with Kuwait, is the newest deep-conversion plant in the region.

countries.name: Peru
countries.slate_detail: Imported heavy and domestic jungle crude
countries.note: Talara's rebuild gave Petroperú a modern coker — and a debt problem large enough to threaten the company.

countries.name: Romania
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Urals-like grades and Black Sea imports
countries.note: Petrobrazi and Petromidia; Lukoil's ownership of Petrotel has made it a sanctions pressure point.

countries.name: Ukraine
countries.slate_detail: Historically Urals and Azeri crude
countries.note: Kremenchuk, the only significant refinery, has been repeatedly struck since 2022. Product supply is now overwhelmingly imported.

countries.name: Chile
countries.slate_detail: Fully imported — Ecuadorian, Brazilian and West African grades
countries.note: ENAP's Aconcagua and Bío Bío; no domestic crude of consequence.

countries.name: Turkmenistan
countries.slate_detail: Domestic light sweet Caspian crude
countries.note: Turkmenbashi is landlocked and export-constrained.

countries.name: Australia
countries.slate_detail: Regional and Middle East light sweet
countries.note: Only Geelong (Viva) and Lytton (Ampol) survive after four closures since 2020. Australia now imports the large majority of its fuel.

countries.name: Norway
countries.slate_detail: Domestic North Sea grades including Johan Sverdrup (28°/0.8% S)
countries.note: Mongstad is the sole significant refinery; Slagen closed in 2021. Sverdrup is medium and slightly sour — heavier than most people assume Norwegian crude to be.

countries.name: Portugal
countries.slate_detail: West African and North Sea grades
countries.note: Galp's Sines is the only remaining refinery after Matosinhos closed in 2021.

countries.name: Uzbekistan
countries.slate_detail: Domestic condensate and light crude
countries.note: Bukhara and Fergana; gas-condensate led.

countries.name: South Africa
countries.slate_detail: Historically imported Middle East and West African crude
countries.note: Nameplate flatters reality: Sapref is shut, Engen's Durban plant converted to a terminal, and Natref is the main survivor. South Africa is now heavily import-dependent.

countries.name: Finland
countries.slate_detail: North Sea and non-Russian grades since 2022
countries.note: Neste's Porvoo is complex and increasingly oriented toward renewable feedstock alongside crude.

countries.name: Morocco
countries.slate_detail: Formerly imported Middle East grades
countries.note: Samir, the sole refinery, has been idle since 2015. Morocco imports all its products.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Azeri Light (35°/0.15% S)
countries.note: Heydar Aliyev refinery at Baku; modernised to Euro-5 specification.

countries.name: Austria
countries.slate_detail: Caspian, North African and Middle East grades via Trieste
countries.note: OMV's Schwechat is inland and pipeline-fed from the Adriatic.

countries.name: Bulgaria
countries.slate_detail: Urals historically; Middle East and Kazakh grades since 2024
countries.note: Lukoil Neftohim Burgas held the EU's last major Urals exemption. It was placed under state-appointed management in 2025 — the sharpest example of a refinery's crude design becoming a sovereignty question.

countries.name: Lithuania
countries.slate_detail: Seaborne grades via Būtingė since Druzhba supply was cut in 2006
countries.note: Orlen Lietuva at Mažeikiai is the Baltic states' only refinery and has been a strategic asset in every regional energy dispute since.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.slate_detail: North Sea grades
countries.note: Fredericia (Shell/Postlane) is the last Danish refinery after Kalundborg's closure was announced.

countries.name: Philippines
countries.slate_detail: Middle East sour and regional sweet
countries.note: Petron's Limay plant is the only refinery since Shell converted Tabangao to an import terminal in 2020.

countries.name: Czechia
countries.slate_detail: Urals via Druzhba historically; now shifting to TAL pipeline supply from Trieste
countries.note: Orlen Unipetrol's Litvínov and Kralupy. The TAL-Plus expansion was explicitly built to end Russian dependence.

countries.name: Ecuador
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Oriente and Napo heavy sour
countries.note: Esmeraldas is the largest; chronic maintenance problems keep utilisation low.

countries.name: Brunei
countries.slate_detail: Regional light sweet
countries.note: Hengyi's Pulau Muara Besar plant is Chinese-owned and export-oriented — a Belt and Road refining outpost.

countries.name: Hungary
countries.slate_detail: Still Urals via Druzhba under EU exemption
countries.note: MOL's Százhalombatta was engineered specifically for Urals; converting it fully to seaborne alternatives is a multi-year capital programme.

countries.name: Trinidad & Tobago
countries.slate_detail: Domestic and imported grades
countries.note: Pointe-à-Pierre has been shut since 2018; repeated sale processes have failed.

countries.name: Cuba
countries.slate_detail: Venezuelan and domestic heavy crude
countries.note: Cienfuegos and Havana run far below nameplate; fuel scarcity is chronic.

countries.name: Slovakia
countries.slate_detail: Urals via Druzhba
countries.note: MOL's Slovnaft at Bratislava, like Hungary's Danube refinery, was built for Russian crude and still runs it under exemption.

countries.name: Angola
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Girassol and Cabinda light sweet
countries.note: Luanda is small and simple; the long-delayed Lobito and Cabinda projects would change the picture if completed.

countries.name: Sudan
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Nile and Dar Blend
countries.note: Khartoum refinery has been damaged in the civil war. Dar Blend is unusually acidic, limiting where it can be processed.

countries.name: Serbia
countries.slate_detail: Seaborne grades via the JANAF pipeline
countries.note: NIS Pančevo is majority Gazprom-owned and was hit by US sanctions in 2025, threatening its crude supply through Croatia.

countries.name: Croatia
countries.slate_detail: Seaborne Mediterranean and Caspian grades
countries.note: INA's Rijeka refinery; Sisak has been converted. JANAF's pipeline gives Croatia leverage over landlocked neighbours.

countries.name: Côte d'Ivoire
countries.slate_detail: West African light sweet
countries.note: SIR at Abidjan supplies much of francophone West Africa.

countries.name: Switzerland
countries.slate_detail: Pipeline-fed Mediterranean grades
countries.note: Cressier is the only remaining refinery.

countries.name: Bolivia
countries.slate_detail: Domestic light condensate-rich crude
countries.note: Small plants at Cochabamba and Santa Cruz; chronic diesel import dependence.

countries.name: Uruguay
countries.slate_detail: Imported West African and Middle East grades
countries.note: ANCAP's La Teja is the country's sole refinery.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
countries.slate_detail: Middle East and Russian grades
countries.note: Sapugaskanda is small and simple; the proposed Hambantota project would dwarf it.

countries.name: Ghana
countries.slate_detail: Domestic Jubilee light sweet
countries.note: Tema Oil Refinery operates intermittently.

countries.name: Bangladesh
countries.slate_detail: Middle East sour term supply
countries.note: Eastern Refinery in Chattogram; an expansion has been under discussion for a decade.

countries.name: Tunisia
countries.slate_detail: Imported and domestic crude
countries.note: Bizerte is small and supplies domestic demand only.

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.note: Marsden Point ceased refining in 2022 and now operates as an import terminal. Nameplate capacity is zero.

refineries.name: Jamnagar (DTA + SEZ)
refineries.slate_detail: Heaviest, sourest barrels available — Urals, Basrah Heavy, Merey, West African
refineries.note: The largest and most complex refinery in the world. Built explicitly to arbitrage crude quality discounts.

refineries.name: Paraguaná (Amuay + Cardón)
refineries.note: Nameplate second-largest in the world; actual runs have been a small fraction for years.

refineries.name: Ulsan
refineries.slate_detail: Middle East medium and heavy sour
refineries.note: Korea's largest; deep conversion and petrochemical integration.

refineries.name: Ruwais
refineries.slate_detail: Murban light sour and Upper Zakum medium sour
refineries.note: Being expanded toward crude-to-chemicals; among the largest single sites globally.

refineries.name: Zhoushan (Phases I–II)
refineries.note: Private, coastal and petrochemical-first — the template for China's new build.

refineries.name: Yeosu
refineries.note: Very high conversion; large export orientation.

refineries.name: Onsan
refineries.note: Aramco-controlled outlet for Saudi sour crude; the Shaheen crude-to-chemicals project is attached.

refineries.name: Dangote
refineries.slate_detail: Nigerian Bonny Light and Qua Iboe, US WTI Midland, Libyan Sharara
refineries.note: Largest single-train refinery ever built. Turned Nigeria from gasoline importer to product exporter; feedstock supply is the binding constraint.

refineries.name: Galveston Bay
refineries.slate_detail: Heavy sour with light shale blending
refineries.note: Largest US refinery. Formerly BP Texas City.

refineries.name: Port Arthur
refineries.slate_detail: Arab Heavy and other Gulf sour grades
refineries.note: Aramco's flagship US outlet — the clearest example of a producer buying downstream placement for its own barrel.

refineries.name: Al-Zour
refineries.slate_detail: Kuwait Export Blend and heavier domestic streams
refineries.note: Purpose-built to turn high-sulphur residue into IMO 2020-compliant low-sulphur fuel oil.

refineries.name: Beaumont
refineries.slate_detail: Permian light sweet plus heavy sour blend
refineries.note: Expanded by 250 kb/d in 2023 — one of very few US capacity additions this decade.

refineries.name: Garyville
refineries.note: Mississippi River plant with deep coking capacity.

refineries.name: Jurong / Pulau Ayer Chawan
refineries.slate_detail: Imported Middle East sour and regional grades
refineries.note: Singapore's largest; fully integrated with olefins.

refineries.name: Baytown
refineries.slate_detail: Light shale and heavy sour blend
refineries.note: One of the oldest large US sites, continuously expanded since 1919.

refineries.name: Ras Tanura
refineries.note: Aramco's original refinery, adjacent to the world's largest crude export terminal.

refineries.name: Mailiao
refineries.note: Wholly petrochemical-integrated; the anchor of Taiwan's plastics industry.

refineries.name: Baton Rouge
refineries.note: Gulf Coast coking plant, among the largest in the US.

refineries.name: SATORP Jubail
refineries.note: Full-conversion plant designed specifically to upgrade Arab Heavy into clean products.

refineries.name: Zhenhai
refineries.slate_detail: Middle East sour and Russian grades
refineries.note: Sinopec's largest, at Ningbo.

refineries.name: Whiting
refineries.slate_detail: Western Canadian Select and other Canadian heavy
refineries.note: Rebuilt for Canadian heavy crude; the Midwest's key coker.

refineries.name: Omsk
refineries.note: Russia's largest and one of only two major refineries not struck by drones as of mid-2026.

refineries.name: Dalian
refineries.slate_detail: Russian ESPO and Middle East sour
refineries.note: Northeastern anchor plant, pipeline-connected to Russian supply.

refineries.name: Pernis
refineries.slate_detail: North Sea, West African and Middle East blend
refineries.note: Europe's largest refinery and one of its most complex.

refineries.name: Vadinar
refineries.note: Sanctioned by the EU in 2025, forcing a shift to domestic sales and non-Western shipping and insurance.

refineries.name: Hengli Changxing
refineries.slate_detail: Middle East sour and Russian ESPO
refineries.note: Private crude-to-chemicals complex built in under three years.

refineries.name: Yulong
refineries.slate_detail: Sanctioned and discounted grades among others
refineries.note: Shandong's flagship consolidation project, started up in 2025 as older teapot capacity was retired.

refineries.name: Jazan
refineries.note: Integrated with a gasification and power complex — residue becomes electricity and hydrogen.

refineries.name: Sitra
refineries.slate_detail: Bahrain field crude and Saudi Arab Light
refineries.note: The Bapco Modernisation Programme lifted both capacity and conversion depth.

refineries.name: Pascagoula
refineries.slate_detail: Heavy sour, including Latin American grades
refineries.note: Chevron's largest US plant, with substantial base-oil production.

refineries.name: Kirishi
refineries.note: Russia's principal supplier of diesel to the Baltic; struck repeatedly in 2025–26.

refineries.name: Ryazan
refineries.note: Supplies the Moscow region; primary units disabled by drone strikes in 2026.

refineries.name: Olmeca (Dos Bocas)
refineries.note: Built to keep Maya at home; ramp-up has been years behind schedule.

refineries.name: Deer Park
refineries.note: Pemex bought out Shell's half in 2022 — a producer securing conversion capacity abroad.

refineries.name: Kstovo (Nizhny Novgorod)
refineries.note: Major gasoline supplier to central Russia; repeatedly struck.

refineries.name: Płock
refineries.slate_detail: Saudi Arab Light and Norwegian grades
refineries.note: Central Europe's largest. Switched off Urals from 2023 largely via Aramco term supply.

refineries.name: Saint John
refineries.slate_detail: Imported light sweet and some Canadian crude
refineries.note: Canada's largest refinery — and it faces the Atlantic, not the oil sands.

refineries.name: ISAB Priolo
refineries.note: Forcibly divested from Lukoil in 2023. One of the few genuinely deep-conversion plants in Europe.

refineries.name: Pengerang RAPID
refineries.note: Modern, complex and petrochemical-integrated; Aramco exited its stake in 2025.

refineries.name: Volgograd
refineries.note: Southern Russia's largest; a repeated drone target.

refineries.name: Panipat
refineries.note: Northern India's main supply point, with a large naphtha cracker attached.

refineries.name: Paradip
refineries.note: Designed from the outset for very sour feed, with a full coker.

refineries.name: STAR Aliağa
refineries.note: Modern and complex; a key node in Turkey's post-2022 product re-export trade.

refineries.name: Duqm
refineries.note: A joint Omani–Kuwaiti plant on the Arabian Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

refineries.name: Schwedt (PCK)
refineries.slate_detail: Kazakh, Norwegian and US grades replacing Urals
refineries.note: Built for Druzhba pipeline Urals; its post-2022 feedstock problem is a live German political issue.

refineries.name: Sines
refineries.slate_detail: West African and North Sea grades
refineries.note: Portugal's only refinery since Matosinhos closed.

refineries.name: Mongstad
refineries.slate_detail: North Sea grades including Johan Sverdrup
refineries.note: Norway's sole significant refinery.

refineries.name: Százhalombatta (Danube)
refineries.note: Still running Russian crude under EU exemption; conversion to seaborne supply is a multi-year programme.

refineries.name: Litvínov
refineries.slate_detail: Shifting from Druzhba Urals to TAL pipeline crude from Trieste
refineries.note: The TAL-Plus capacity expansion was built expressly to end Czech dependence on Russian crude.
